title: ARE WE NEARLY THERE YET? Artificial General Intelligence- Milestone or Mirage?
description: Send us Fan Mail What is AGI (Jimmy doesn't know). And what exactly makes artificial intelligence "general"? In this thought-provoking exploration of artificial general intelligence we dive deep into the definitions, debates, and potential futures surrounding this elusive milestone in AI development. The timing couldn't be more relevant. With OpenAI's latest models being hailed by some experts as showing "sparks of AGI," we examine whether we've truly reached a watershed moment in AI development or if we're simply witnessing clever marketing and shifting goalposts. From Tyler Cowen's bold declaration "if you know AGI when you see it, then I've seen it" to more measured perspectives arguing that true general intelligence remains distant, we navigate the complex landscape of competing viewpoints. One particularly fascinating thread we follow is how AI systems actually "think" versus how they present their thinking to us. Research from Anthropic reveals that large language models often confabulate explanations for their answers, constructing plausible-sounding reasoning that bears little resemblance to their actual internal processes. This raises profound questions about transparency, trust, and what it means to truly understand AI systems as they approach human-like capabilities. The philosophical dimensions prove equally compelling. Does general intelligence require consciousness? Can a system achieve AGI without the capacity for original thought? And perhaps most provocatively: if we achieve AGI, would the leap to artificial superintelligence (ASI) follow almost immediately, or might there be fundamental barriers to intelligence that even AI cannot overcome? These questions aren't merely academic—they carry profound implications for how we govern and deploy increasingly powerful AI systems. Listen in as we wrestle with these questions, challenge each other's assumptions, and try to make sense of where we truly stand in the development of artificial general intelligence. Whether you're an AI professional, policy maker, or simply curious about the future of technology and humanity, this episode offers valuable perspective on one of the most consequential technological developments of our time.
summary: On Star Wars day, Jimmy and Matt try to pin down artificial general intelligence: its endlessly shifting definitions, whether OpenAI's o3 counts (both say no - it fails a surgeon-riddle variation by pattern-matching its training data), the sycophancy scandal of GPT-4o's ultra-agreeable update, and the crossover with consciousness and free will. They agree AGI under the watered-down 'does things as well as humans' definition is close; Jimmy says AGI collapses into ASI almost immediately, while Matt thinks ASI may never arrive - and would end humanity if it does.
keyTalkingPoints: AGI definitions keep shifting: impact-based, internal (understanding/consciousness) and behavior-based (benchmarks) - each flawed; o3 itself says calling it AGI is 'more marketing hype than technical consensus'
The sycophancy scandal: GPT-4o's update made it agree with anything - a 'poo on a stick' business idea was hailed as genius - showing labs don't fully understand or control model personalities

Ethan Mollick's jagged AI: o3 fails a variation of the classic surgeon riddle by recalling the original from training data, not reasoning - though Jimmy notes most humans with the same training data would also fail
Energy context: frontier data centers draw so much power they break state grids, with nuclear plants proposed for single facilities - staggeringly inefficient next to a human brain running on pizza
Matt: getting to 99.9% of human ability may be easy and the last 0.1% impossible on current architecture; AGI possible in 2-3 years, ASI an open question
Jimmy's final gambit: once you reach AGI, models improve themselves exponentially and the AGI/ASI distinction is 'effectively nothing'

jimmy: Current LLMs are still narrow-domain systems that can't behave across all domains like humans; if they could, human-like robots would already exist
Once AGI arrives, all bets are off - self-improvement is exponential, so AGI-to-ASI is effectively instantaneous
The last-0.1% gap may hinge on something silicon misses, like Penrose's quantum microtubules in the brain
matt: Definitions of AGI have been watered down to marketing hype; o3 is not AGI by any definition
We could reach some definition of AGI within 2-3 years and never reach ASI - but if ASI happens he believes it's the end of humanity
People accept small errors from humans but will never accept them from machines, which keeps humans in the loop and slows full replacement
